mainTopic: Collecting from sold land when free land is ruined, אביי's rulings on a gift of 'to you, and after you to so-and-so' when the woman marries, and the opening of the chapter on a widow's support
overview: The amud opens by challenging the view that a creditor cannot collect from buyers when the debtor's free land is ruined. The challenge is the everyday case of an orchard that aged early, where the רבנן let the lender collect from buyers. The גמרא answers that those buyers knew orchards grow old, so they brought the loss on themselves. Still, the הלכה is that when free property is ruined, the creditor collects from sold property. Next, אביי rules that in a gift of 'to you, and after you to so-and-so,' if the woman marries, her husband counts as a לוקח and the second recipient gets nothing. This follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and the גמרא shows how it fits with אביי calling it wicked to advise such sales. In a second ruling, when the woman sells and dies, the claims go in a circle, but the property stays with the buyer, since only he paid money. רב אשי settles the clash between the two rulings: it depends on whether she was single or already married when the gift was given. The chapter closes by explaining 'and so too a creditor.' A new chapter then opens on a widow's support, and the גמרא asks whether the משנה reads ניזונת or הניזונת.

steps.title: Challenge from the everyday case of the aging orchard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the view that ruined free land does not let a creditor go to the buyers, using a well-known case where the רבנן did let him.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this happens every day! A man mortgaged his orchard to his friend for ten years, and after five years the orchard grew old. The friend came before the רבנן, and they wrote him a טירפא, a document that lets him collect from land the debtor had sold.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the position just discussed by pointing to a common real-life case that seems to show the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender was supposed to be paid from the orchard's fruit for ten years. When the orchard stopped producing after five, the רבנן let him collect from land the debtor had sold to others. That looks like proof that when free property is ruined, the creditor may go after sold property.

keyTerms.meaning: It happens every day; a common, accepted practice
Mortgaged; gave as a pledge for a loan
An orchard
Grew old; stopped producing well
A court document allowing a creditor to seize sold, liened land

phrases.english: But there are cases like this every day,
that a certain man mortgaged
an orchard to his fellow for ten years,
and it grew old after five years,
and he came before the Rabbis,
and they wrote him a document of repossession!
phrases.notes: This document lets him collect from land the debtor sold to buyers after the loan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the view, from before this section, that ruined free property does not open the way to collect from buyers.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that when free property (בני חרי) is ruined, the creditor still cannot collect from sold property.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Common court practice in the orchard case allowed collecting from buyers when the free property stopped producing, which seems to contradict that view.

steps.title: The buyers knew orchards grow old
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that in the orchard case the buyers caused their own loss, because everyone knows orchards age.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, the buyers brought the loss on themselves. Since they knew an orchard tends to grow old, they should not have bought the land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the original view by explaining why the orchard case is special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An orchard's aging is predictable, so buyers should have expected the creditor might not be fully paid from it. Because they were warned in a sense, it is fair that the creditor collects from them. That is different from a sudden, unexpected ruin, so the orchard case does not prove the general rule.

keyTerms.meaning: There too; the same reasoning applies in that case
They caused the loss to themselves
To buy

phrases.english: There too,
it was they who caused the loss to themselves,
phrases.notes: "They" means the buyers who bought land from the debtor.

phrases.english: since they knew
that an orchard tends to grow old,
they should not have bought.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי, אִינְהוּ הוּא דְּאַפְסִידוּ אַנַּפְשַׁיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1 by limiting the orchard case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: the orchard's aging was predictable, so the buyers are at fault.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The orchard case shows that any ruin of free property lets the creditor collect from buyers.
steps.terutzMaskana: The orchard case is special because buyers knew orchards age; it does not prove a general rule.

steps.title: Final ruling: ruined free property lets the creditor collect from sold property
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that if the debtor's free property is ruined, the creditor may collect from liened property.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: if the free property became blighted, the creditor collects from the liened property.
steps.whatsHappening: After the back-and-forth, the גמרא gives the final practical ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the orchard case was answered, the הלכה still follows the side that lets the creditor collect from buyers. The creditor is not stuck with ruined land just because there was free property when the land was sold.

keyTerms.meaning: And the practical law is
Became blighted or ruined
Free property; land the debtor still owns, not sold
Liened property; land sold to others but still tied to the debt

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה: if the debtor's free property (בני חרי) is ruined, the creditor may collect from property that was sold (משעבדי).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think step 2's answer decides the הלכה. Step 2 only defends one view against the orchard proof; the final ruling in step 3 goes the other way.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical rule of debt collection: buyers of a debtor's land can lose it if the debtor's remaining land becomes worthless.

phrases.english: And the halacha is:
if the free property became blighted,
one collects from liened property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion with the final ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When free property is ruined, the creditor may seize liened property from buyers.

steps.title: אביי: a gift 'to you and after you to so-and-so' and the woman marries
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules that when the woman who received the gift marries, her husband counts as a buyer and the second recipient gets nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: If someone said, 'My property is yours, and after you it goes to so-and-so,' and she went and married, the husband counts as a buyer, and the 'after you' person gets nothing when there is a husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from אביי about a gift with a second recipient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a gift of 'to you, and after you to so-and-so,' the first recipient may still sell the property, and the sale stands. A husband is treated like a לוקח of his wife's property. So when she marries, it is as if she sold it to him, and the second recipient has nothing left to get.

keyTerms.meaning: And after you, to so-and-so; naming a second recipient
She married
The husband is considered a buyer
Where there is a husband

steps.whatToRemember: אביי: in a gift of 'to you and after you to so-and-so,' if the woman marries, her husband is like a buyer, and the 'after you' person gets nothing.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
"My property is to you, and after you to so-and-so,"
phrases.notes: A man says this to an unmarried woman when giving her his property.

phrases.english: and she went and married,
the husband is a buyer,
and the "after you" person has
nothing where there is a husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the ruling on ruined free property.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a woman who received property 'and after you to so-and-so' marries, her husband is like a buyer and the second recipient receives nothing.

steps.title: Whose view is אביי following?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which תנא אביי's ruling about the husband matches.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which earlier opinion אביי's ruling in step 4 is based on. This short question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4, אביי said the husband counts as a buyer, so the second recipient gets nothing. That only works if what the first recipient does with the property can cancel the second recipient's rights. So the גמרא wants to know which תנא holds that way.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom? (which opinion is this based on)

phrases.english: According to whom?
phrases.notes: He means: which תנא is אביי's ruling from the step before based on?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks which earlier source אביי's ruling in step 4 rests on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא holds that the first recipient's actions can cancel the second recipient's rights, as אביי's ruling assumes.

steps.title: אביי follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a מחלוקת between רבי and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל about a first recipient who sold the property. אביי follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like this תנא, as a ברייתא teaches: if someone says 'My property is yours, and after you it goes to so-and-so,' and the first recipient sold it, רבי says the second recipient can take it back from the buyers. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the second recipient gets only what the first one left over.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אביי follows one side of a ברייתא. Its case is a gift to one person that passes to another person after the first one dies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי holds the first recipient only has the right to use the property, so a sale does not work against the second recipient. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds the first recipient can sell it, and the second gets only what remains. אביי's ruling that the husband (a kind of buyer) beats the second recipient fits רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: 'My property is yours, and after you, to so-and-so': a gift that passes to a second person after the first
The first recipient / the second recipient
Takes the property back from the buyers
What he left over

steps.whyThisMatters: This מחלוקת is the base for every ruling in the rest of this passage about the husband, the buyer and the second recipient.

phrases.english: Like this תנא,
as it was taught in a ברייתא:
"My property is yours, and after you, to so-and-so,"
and the first one went ahead and sold it:
phrases.notes: Literally 'went down'. He means the first recipient took over the property and sold it.

phrases.english: the second one takes it back from the buyers,
these are the words of רבי.
רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says:
the second one has nothing except
what the first one left over.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5 by quoting a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אביי follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who holds that the second recipient gets only what the first recipient left.

steps.title: אביי called advising such a sale wicked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this: אביי himself called a person who advises selling such property a clever wicked person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did אביי really say this? But אביי said: Who is a clever wicked person? Someone who gives advice to sell property according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that אביי would rule in a way that helps the first recipient block the second recipient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי condemned anyone who advises the first recipient to use the רבן שמעון בן גמליאל rule to cut out the second recipient. If he disapproves of that, how can he rule that marrying, which acts like a sale, takes the property away from the second recipient?

keyTerms.meaning: A clever (sly) wicked person
One who gives advice

steps.confusionAlert: אביי does not say the sale is invalid. He agrees it works according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. He only says it is wicked to advise someone to do it.

phrases.english: And did אביי really say this?
But אביי said:
Who is a clever wicked person?
This is one who gives advice
to sell property
according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל!
phrases.notes: He means advising the first recipient to sell so that nothing is left for the second one.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר אַבָּיֵי הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר אַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the step 6 conclusion that אביי follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל to the second recipient's loss.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's ruling (step 4) that the husband beats the second recipient
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אביי elsewhere condemns using רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's rule to deprive the second recipient. That seems to clash with his ruling that defeats the second recipient.

steps.title: He spoke of a woman who already married
steps.stepSummary: אביי never said to advise her to marry. He ruled about a woman who simply got married.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did he say 'she should marry'? He said 'she married.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that אביי's ruling covers what happens after a woman marries. It is not advice to marry in order to cut out the second recipient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Getting married is the normal course of life, not a trick against the second recipient. The result follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, but no one schemed to bring it about. What אביי condemned was giving scheming advice, not the legal outcome itself.

keyTerms.meaning: She should marry (advice for the future)
She married (something that already happened)

phrases.english: Did he say 'she should marry'?
He said 'she married.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: a past event versus advice to act
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי's ruling seemed to approve of using marriage as a scheme to deprive the second recipient.
steps.terutzMaskana: אביי only describes the legal result once a woman has naturally married. He never endorsed advising her to marry for that purpose.

steps.title: The circle: buyer, husband, and the second recipient
steps.stepSummary: אביי rules on a case where the woman sold the property and died. The husband takes from the buyers, the second recipient takes from the husband, and the buyer takes from the second recipient. In the end the property stays with the buyer.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי also said: if someone said 'My property is yours, and after you to so-and-so,' and she sold it and died, the husband takes it from the buyers. The 'after you' person takes it from the husband. The buyer takes it from the 'after you' person. And we leave all of it in the buyer's hands.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a new ruling on a married woman who received such a gift, sold it, and then died. The claims go around in a circle, and אביי himself rules that the property stays with the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each party has a claim that beats the next one. The husband counts as an earlier buyer than the purchaser. The 'after you' person has a claim against the husband. The purchaser has a claim against the 'after you' person because he bought it from the woman herself. אביי rules that the property stays with the buyer, and step 11 explains why: only the buyer paid money.

keyTerms.meaning: The husband
The buyer
And we establish (leave it in place)
In the hands of the buyer

steps.whatToRemember: In the circular case (she sold, then died), husband beats buyer, 'after you' beats husband, and buyer beats 'after you'. The property ends up staying with the buyer.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for one claimant who is 'strongest'. Each claim beats only the next person in the circle, which is why the גמרא has to stop the loop at the buyer.

phrases.english: And אביי said:
"My property is yours, and after you, to so-and-so,"
and she sold it and died:
the husband takes it back from the buyers,
and 'after you' takes it from the husband,
and the buyer takes it from 'after you.'
And we leave all of it in the buyer's hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר אַבָּיֵי: ״נְכָסַי לִיךְ וְאַחֲרַיִךְ לִפְלוֹנִי״ וּמָכְרָה וָמֵתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new ruling by אביי on the same kind of gift, now with a sale before the woman's death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a married woman who received a chain gift sells the property and dies, the claims go in a circle (husband over buyer, 'after you' over husband, buyer over 'after you'), and the property is left with the buyer.

steps.title: Why doesn't אביי's case end in a compromise like the משנה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contrasts אביי's ruling with the משנה, where the claims go around in a circle until the sides make a פשרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from what we learned in the משנה: they keep going around in a circle until they make a compromise between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's ruling. In the משנה, a circle of claims ends in a פשרה, so why does אביי say the property just stays with the buyer?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9, אביי described a circle of claims: husband, then second recipient, then buyer. He ruled that the property stays with the buyer. But the משנה also describes a circle of claims, and there the parties must reach a פשרה. So why should אביי's circle end differently?

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? It asks why two similar cases get different rulings.
They go around in a circle, with each claim leading back to the previous one.
A compromise between the parties.

phrases.english: What is different from that which we learned:
and they go around in a circle
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה about a man with two wives who sold his field: the two wives and the buyer keep taking it from each other.

phrases.english: until they make a compromise between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the outcome of אביי's ruling in step 9 by comparing it to the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's ruling that the property ends up staying with the buyer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה has a similar circle of claims and rules that the parties must make a פשרה. So אביי's circle should also end in a פשרה, not in a clear win for the buyer.

steps.title: Only the buyer stands to lose money
steps.stepSummary: In the משנה, every party paid or is owed money. In אביי's case, only the buyer paid, so the property goes to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, all of them stand to lose. Here, only the buyer stands to lose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two cases are different. In the משנה everyone stands to lose money, but in אביי's case only the buyer does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the buyer paid for the field and both wives have real money claims for their כתובות, so a פשרה is fair. In אביי's case, the husband and the second recipient got the property as a gift and paid nothing. Only the buyer would truly lose, so the property stays with him.

keyTerms.meaning: A loss, meaning money a person would actually lose.
A buyer who paid money for the property.

steps.whatToRemember: A circle of claims ends in a פשרה only when every side stands to lose. When only the buyer stands to lose, the property stays with him.

phrases.english: There, all of them have a loss,
here, it is the buyer
who has a loss.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by who actually stands to lose money.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The challenger thought that any circle of claims must end in a פשרה.
steps.terutzMaskana: A פשרה is needed only when every party stands to lose. When only the buyer does, he keeps the property.

steps.title: רפרם's challenge: אביי called the husband a buyer
steps.stepSummary: רפרם reports אביי's ruling to רב אשי and points to another ruling of אביי, where the husband counts as a לוקח and the second recipient gets nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רפרם went and said this teaching before רב אשי. Did אביי really say this? But אביי said: if someone says, "My property is yours, and after you it goes to so-and-so," and she got married, the husband counts as a buyer, and "after you" gets nothing where there is a husband.
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם brings אביי's ruling to רב אשי and raises a contradiction. In another ruling, אביי said the husband counts as a לוקח and blocks the second recipient entirely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9, the second recipient was able to take the property from the husband. But in this other ruling, the husband counts as a לוקח, and the second recipient gets nothing at all. These two rulings of אביי seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching or ruling.
"My property is yours, and after you it goes to so-and-so." This is a gift with a second recipient lined up next.
"After you," meaning the second recipient.
The husband counts as a buyer.

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the same as step 7. There, the challenge was about advising someone to sell. Here, the problem is the husband's status as a לוקח.

phrases.english: Rafram went and said this teaching
before Rav Ashi.
Did Abaye really say this?
But didn't Abaye say:
"My property is to you, and after you to so-and-so,"
and she went and got married —
the husband is a buyer,
and "after you" has nothing where there is a husband.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמַר אַבָּיֵי הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר אַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against אביי's ruling in step 9, based on his own earlier ruling in step 4 that the husband counts as a לוקח.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's ruling in step 9 that the second recipient takes the property from the husband.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אביי himself ruled that a husband counts as a לוקח, so the second recipient gets nothing. That contradicts the second recipient taking from the husband in step 9.

steps.title: Single when given versus already married
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that it depends on when the gift was given. If she was single, the husband wins. If she was already married, the giver meant to keep the husband out.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: there, he said it to her while she was single. Here, he said it to her while she was married. What he is telling her is that "after you" should acquire, and the husband should not.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי settles the contradiction by pointing to when the gift was given. Was the woman still single, or already married?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the giver spoke while she was single, he did not plan around a husband. Then the husband later becomes a לוקח and wins. If she was already married, the giver knew her husband would normally inherit her. By naming someone for "after you," he clearly meant that person to get it instead of the husband.

keyTerms.meaning: An unmarried woman.
A married woman.
Should acquire.

steps.whatToRemember: The husband counts as a לוקח against the second recipient only if the gift was given before the marriage. If it was given during the marriage, the giver meant to keep the husband out.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי answering רפרם.

phrases.english: There, it is where he said it to her when she was unmarried,
here, it is where he said it to her when she was married.
What is he saying to her?
"After you" should acquire,
the husband should not acquire.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by when the gift was given: before or during the marriage.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רפרם thought the husband always counts as a לוקח and always blocks the second recipient.
steps.terutzMaskana: The husband blocks the second recipient only if the gift was given while she was single. If it was given while she was married, the second recipient wins.

steps.title: Explaining 'and so too a creditor'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words וכן בעל חוב and explains them with a ברייתא: the same circle applies to a creditor and two buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says, "And so too a creditor." It was taught in a ברייתא: and so too a creditor and two buyers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new phrase in the משנה. It quotes a ברייתא to show what case the words וכן בעל חוב mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the same circle of claims happens with a בעל חוב whose debtor sold fields to two buyers. If the creditor gives up his claim against the second buyer, the claims go around in a circle just like with the wife. So the parties must make a פשרה.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone who is owed money.
It was taught. This introduces a ברייתא.
Two buyers.

phrases.english: And so too a creditor.
It was taught:
And so too a creditor and two buyers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of אביי and returns to explaining the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's words וכן בעל חוב refer to a creditor and two buyers. The same circle of claims applies there until the parties make a פשרה.

steps.title: The same circle applies to a woman collecting her כתובה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes: a woman owed her כתובה, together with two buyers, works the same way as a creditor and two buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the same is true of a woman who is owed money and two buyers.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא that explains the משנה's words וכן בעל חוב finishes its last line. It adds one more case that works like the creditor case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman collecting her כתובה from her husband's sold property is treated like any creditor. So when there are two buyers, the same circle of claims and the same פשרה apply to her.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman who is a creditor, here meaning a wife collecting her כתובה
Buyers of the husband's property

steps.whatToRemember: The circle of claims in the משנה applies to a regular creditor and also to a woman collecting her כתובה, whenever two buyers are involved.

phrases.english: And so too, a woman who is a creditor
phrases.notes: He means a wife collecting her כתובה from what her husband owned. Her כתובה is a debt he owes her.

phrases.english: and two buyers.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן אִשָּׁה בַּעֲלַת חוֹב וּשְׁנֵי לָקוֹחוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא quoted in step 14 by adding the case of a woman collecting her כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman collecting her כתובה, together with two buyers, is handled like a creditor with two buyers.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing מי שהיה נשוי
steps.stepSummary: The chapter מי שהיה נשוי ends.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'One who was married'.
steps.whatsHappening: This line marks the end of the chapter. It is a closing formula, not part of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is taught here. It signals that the discussion of a man with several wives and their כתובות is finished, and a new topic is about to begin.

steps.title: New chapter: a widow's food, earnings and burial
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a widow is fed from the orphans' property and her earnings belong to them. Her burial is the duty of the heirs who inherit her כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A widow is fed from the property of the orphans. What she earns belongs to them, and they do not have to pay for her burial. Her heirs, the ones who inherit her כתובה, must pay for her burial.
steps.whatsHappening: A new chapter opens with a משנה about a widow living off her late husband's estate. It sets out who gets her earnings and who pays to bury her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the orphans feed her, her earnings go to them, just as a wife's earnings went to her husband. Burial, though, is linked to her כתובה. Whoever inherits the כתובה, her own heirs, must bury her. The orphans are not obligated just because they feed her.

keyTerms.meaning: Widow
Is fed or supported

Her earnings, the work of her hands
Burial

steps.confusionAlert: The 'heirs who inherit her כתובה' are HER heirs. The משנה is contrasting two roles: feeding her from the estate does not bring a burial duty, but inheriting her כתובה does. If the orphans are her own sons, they may fill both roles.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The orphans feed the widow and receive her earnings. Her burial falls on the heirs of her כתובה, not on the orphans as the ones who feed her.

steps.title: Does the משנה say 'is fed' or 'who is fed'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which wording the משנה has, ניזונת or הניזונת. It starts explaining the first option: every widow is fed, following the custom of the people of the גליל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: did we learn 'is fed' or 'the one who is fed'? If we learned 'is fed', the משנה follows the people of the גליל, and the heirs have no choice but to give her food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about the exact wording of the משנה. It then begins to explain what the first possible wording would mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ניזונת' is a flat rule that every widow gets food. 'הניזונת' would mean the משנה only talks about a widow who happens to be fed. If it says ניזונת, the משנה matches the people of the גליל, who wrote the widow's food into the כתובה, so the heirs must always give it.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised among the חכמים
We learned (in the משנה)
The one who is fed
The people of the גליל and their כתובה custom
It is impossible not to; there is no choice

steps.confusionAlert: The whole question hangs on one letter, ה. Without it the משנה states a rule for every widow. With it the משנה only describes a widow who is being fed.

Did we learn 'is fed'
or did we learn 'who is fed'?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the משנה reads ניזונת (every widow is fed) or הניזונת (only a widow who is being fed), and what each reading implies.
steps.whyThisMatters: The wording decides whether the משנה sets a universal right to food or only describes the case of a widow who is already being fed.

steps.title: The second option: the wording is הניזונת, following the people of יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the second side of its question. Maybe the משנה says הניזונת, which follows the custom of the people of יהודה, and the heirs can stop feeding her if they want.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or maybe the משנה says 'the widow who is fed' (הניזונת). That follows the people of יהודה, and if the heirs want, they don't have to give her food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its two-sided question by giving the second possible wording of the משנה. The question stays open here, and the גמרא will try to settle it next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the extra letter ה, the משנה means 'the widow who is being fed', so not every widow is fed. That fits the people of יהודה, where the heirs may pay her כתובה and end her food. The first option (ניזונת, every widow is fed, like the גליל) gave the widow a right the heirs could not take away.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps. This opens the second side of a question.
The one who is being fed. The ה points to a particular widow who receives food, not every widow.

They don't give her (food).

steps.confusionAlert: The two wordings differ by just one letter (ה), yet that letter changes the law: is food the right of every widow, or only of a widow the heirs have not yet paid off?
